questions.explanation_en: Strassen uses 7 block multiplications instead of the naive 8, plus Θ(n²) work for additions. By the Master theorem T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂ 7)) ≈ Θ(n^2.81), better than the Θ(n³) of the 8-multiplication version.

questions.question_en: A knapsack of capacity 15 kg is to be filled from items I1 (5 kg, ₹30), I2 (10 kg, ₹40), I3 (4 kg, ₹28) and I4 (8 kg, ₹24). Items may be broken (fractional knapsack). What is the maximum total value?
questions.explanation_en: Value/weight ratios: I3 = 7, I1 = 6, I2 = 4, I4 = 3. Take I3 (4 kg, ₹28) and I1 (5 kg, ₹30), using 9 kg; the remaining 6 kg is 6/10 of I2, worth ₹24. Maximum value = 28 + 30 + 24 = ₹82.

questions.question_en: Activities (start, finish): A(2, 5), B(1, 3), C(4, 7), D(6, 8), E(3, 9), F(8, 10), G(9, 12), H(11, 13). An activity may start exactly when the previous one finishes. What is the maximum number of activities one person can perform?
questions.explanation_en: Greedy rule: sort by finish time and pick each activity that starts no earlier than the last chosen one finishes. Order by finish: B(3), A(5), C(7), D(8), E(9), F(10), G(12), H(13). The picks are B(1–3), C(4–7), F(8–10) and H(11–13), so 4 activities.

questions.question_en: A message contains the characters P, Q, R, S and T with frequencies 4, 7, 10, 15 and 20. Using Huffman coding, how many bits are needed to encode the whole message?
questions.explanation_en: Merge the two smallest weights each time: 4 + 7 = 11; 10 + 11 = 21; 15 + 20 = 35; 21 + 35 = 56. P and Q get 3-bit codes while R, S and T get 2-bit codes, so the total is 4×3 + 7×3 + 10×2 + 15×2 + 20×2 = 123 bits (also the sum of merges 11 + 21 + 35 + 56). A fixed 3-bit code would need 168 bits.

questions.question_en: Each job takes one unit of time. Jobs (profit, deadline): J1 (35, 3), J2 (30, 4), J3 (25, 4), J4 (20, 2), J5 (15, 3), J6 (12, 1), J7 (5, 2). What is the maximum total profit if each job must finish by its deadline?
questions.explanation_en: Take jobs in decreasing order of profit and place each in the latest free slot not after its deadline. J1 → slot 3, J2 → slot 4, J3 → slot 2, J4 → slot 1; all 4 slots (maximum deadline 4) are now full, so J5, J6 and J7 are rejected. Maximum profit = 35 + 30 + 25 + 20 = 110.

questions.question_en: The greedy method (choosing by value/weight ratio) is guaranteed to give an optimal solution for which version of the knapsack problem?
questions.explanation_en: In the fractional knapsack items can be split, so filling the bag in decreasing order of value/weight is always optimal. In the 0/1 version an item must be taken whole; the same greedy rule can leave capacity unused and miss the best combination, so dynamic programming is used.

questions.question_en: Which two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to be applied effectively?
questions.explanation_en: Optimal substructure means an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of subproblems. Overlapping subproblems means the same subproblems recur, so their answers can be stored (memoised or tabulated) and reused. Divide and conquer, by contrast, works on independent subproblems.

questions.question_en: In a 0/1 knapsack problem the capacity is 9 and the items (weight, value) are (2, 12), (3, 20), (4, 28) and (5, 33). What is the maximum total value?
questions.explanation_en: Taking the items of weight 4 and 5 gives 28 + 33 = 61, while weights 2 + 3 + 4 give 12 + 20 + 28 = 60. Greedy by value/weight ratio (7, 6.67, 6.6, 6) picks weights 4, 3, 2 for only 60, and the DP table confirms 61 as the optimum. 61.2 would be the fractional-knapsack value.

questions.question_en: What is the length of the longest common subsequence (LCS) of the strings ALGORITHM and LOGARITHM?
questions.explanation_en: Both words end in RITHM, and their prefixes are ALGO and LOGA. In these prefixes A comes before L, G and O in one word but after them in the other, and G and O are also in opposite orders, so at least two letters must be dropped. A common subsequence of length 7 exists (e.g., LGRITHM), so the LCS length is 7.

questions.question_en: Sum of subsets problem: w = {3, 5, 6, 7, 9} and the required sum m = 15. Writing each solution as a 0/1 vector (1 = item included), which option lists all the solutions?
questions.explanation_en: The subsets with sum 15 are {3, 5, 7} = 11010 and {6, 9} = 00101; no other subset works. 00110 = 6 + 7 = 13, 10110 = 3 + 6 + 7 = 16 and 10011 = 3 + 7 + 9 = 19, so the other options contain wrong vectors.

questions.question_en: In the 4-queens problem a solution is written as (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄), where xᵢ is the column of the queen in row i. Which of the following is a valid solution?
questions.explanation_en: In (3, 1, 4, 2) all columns differ and |xᵢ − xⱼ| ≠ |i − j| for every pair of rows, so no two queens share a diagonal. Each other option has a diagonal clash, e.g., (1, 4, 2, 3) has queens at rows 3 and 4 in columns 2 and 3. The 4-queens problem has exactly two solutions: (2, 4, 1, 3) and (3, 1, 4, 2).

questions.question_en: Which statement correctly describes branch and bound as compared with backtracking?

options.en: It explores the state-space tree only depth-first
It uses bounds, often with FIFO/least-cost search, to prune
It always finds a solution faster than backtracking
It never prunes any node of the state-space tree

questions.explanation_en: Backtracking searches the state-space tree depth-first and abandons a node as soon as it cannot lead to a feasible solution. Branch and bound is used mainly for optimisation problems (e.g., 0/1 knapsack, travelling salesman): it computes a bound for each live node, expands nodes in FIFO or least-cost order, and prunes nodes that cannot beat the best solution so far.

questions.question_en: Which of the following problems is NP-complete?
questions.explanation_en: SAT was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin theorem). Sorting (O(n log n)), shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm and the MST (Prim/Kruskal) all have polynomial-time algorithms, so they are in P.

questions.question_en: Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.en: P is a subset of NP (P ⊆ NP)
It has been proved that NP ⊆ P
Every NP-hard problem belongs to NP
NP-complete in P would imply P ≠ NP

questions.explanation_en: A problem solvable in polynomial time can also be verified in polynomial time, so P ⊆ NP. Whether NP ⊆ P (i.e., P = NP) is still open. NP-hard problems need not be in NP (the halting problem is NP-hard but undecidable), and if any NP-complete problem were in P, then P = NP.

tests.description: 15 most expected questions on Algorithm Design Techniques, with solutions.

tests.title: DSA — 200 Most Expected Questions (Full Test)
tests.subject: Computer Science

questions.question_en: An algorithm must stop after a finite number of steps for every valid input. Which characteristic of an algorithm does this describe?
questions.explanation_en: Finiteness means the algorithm terminates after a finite number of steps for all valid inputs. Definiteness means each step is clear and unambiguous, and effectiveness means each step is basic enough to be carried out exactly in finite time.

questions.question_en: Which characteristic of an algorithm requires every operation to be so basic that a person could, in principle, carry it out exactly with pencil and paper in a finite time?
questions.explanation_en: This is effectiveness (Horowitz–Sahni): each operation must be basic and actually feasible, not merely well stated. Finiteness is about the whole algorithm stopping, while definiteness is about each step being unambiguous (an instruction like 'add 6 or 7 to x' violates definiteness).

questions.question_en: As per the standard definition of an algorithm (Knuth; Horowitz–Sahni), how many inputs and outputs must an algorithm have?

options.en: At least one input, at least one output
At least one input, zero or more outputs
Exactly one input and exactly one output
Zero or more inputs, at least one output

questions.explanation_en: An algorithm may take zero or more externally supplied inputs; a routine that prints the first 10 primes needs no input at all. But it must produce at least one output, otherwise it does nothing useful.

questions.question_en: In a flowchart, which symbol is used for an input/output step such as 'Read A, B' or 'Print SUM'?
questions.explanation_en: The parallelogram is the input/output symbol. The oval marks Start/Stop, the rectangle is a processing step (e.g., SUM = A + B) and the diamond is a decision with Yes/No branches.

questions.question_en:
Consider the following statements:
(i) Pseudocode has no strict syntax and cannot be executed directly, yet it is easier to convert into a program than a flowchart.
(ii) In a flowchart, the Start and Stop steps are drawn as rectangles.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation_en: (i) is true: pseudocode uses programming-like constructs (IF, WHILE, FOR) without a fixed syntax, so it maps almost line by line to code. (ii) is false: Start and Stop use the oval (terminal) symbol; the rectangle is the processing symbol.

questions.question_en: 'Given a graph G and an integer k, can G be coloured with at most k colours?' The answer to this problem is only YES or NO. Such a problem is called a/an:
questions.explanation_en: A decision problem has a yes/no answer. The related optimisation problem asks for the minimum number of colours (the chromatic number), and an enumeration problem would list every valid colouring.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is an optimisation problem?

options.en: Does any path exist from city P to city Q?
Find the cheapest route from city P to city Q
List every permutation of the set {1, 2, 3}
Is the number 221 a prime number?

questions.explanation_en: An optimisation problem picks the best (minimum or maximum) solution among all feasible ones, and the cheapest route minimises cost over all routes. Path existence and primality are decision (yes/no) problems (221 = 13 × 17), and listing permutations is an enumeration problem.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is a non-linear data structure?
questions.explanation_en: In a linear structure (array, stack, queue, linked list) each element has at most one predecessor and one successor, so the elements form a sequence. In a tree a node can have several children, so it is non-linear; graphs are non-linear too.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is a primitive data structure?
questions.explanation_en: Primitive data structures are the basic types that machine instructions operate on directly: int, char, float, double and pointer. Arrays, structures, linked lists, stacks and trees are non-primitive because they are built from primitive types.

questions.question_en: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) such as 'Stack' is best described as:

options.en: Values and operations, specified without implementation details
A fixed memory layout chosen by the compiler for the data
A data type that can only be implemented using an array
A set of machine instructions written for one processor

questions.explanation_en: An ADT states what data is stored and which operations (e.g., push, pop, isEmpty) are allowed, but not how they are implemented. A stack ADT can be implemented with an array or with a linked list without changing its interface.

questions.question_en: If f(n) = O(g(n)), then g(n) is an asymptotic ______ of f(n).
questions.explanation_en: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are constants c > 0 and n₀ such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀, so g bounds f from above. Ω gives a lower bound and Θ gives a tight (two-sided) bound.

questions.question_en: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if and only if there exist positive constants c₁, c₂ and n₀ such that, for all n ≥ n₀:
questions.explanation_en: Θ is a tight bound: f is sandwiched between c₁·g(n) and c₂·g(n) for all large n. The condition with only the upper constant c₂ defines O, the one with only c₁ defines Ω, and 'f(n) < c·g(n) for every c > 0' defines little-o (a strict upper bound).

questions.question_en: For f(n) = 4n² + 7n log n + 50, which statement is FALSE?
questions.explanation_en: The dominant term is 4n², so f(n) = Θ(n²). Hence f is also O(n³) (a looser upper bound) and Ω(n log n) (a looser lower bound). But n² grows faster than n log n, so f(n) = O(n log n) is false.

questions.question_en:
Arrange the following functions in increasing order of growth:
n!, n log n, 2ⁿ, √n, n³, log n

options.en: log n, n log n, √n, n³, 2ⁿ, n!
√n, log n, n log n, n³, n!, 2ⁿ
log n, √n, n log n, n³, 2ⁿ, n!
log n, √n, n³, n log n, 2ⁿ, n!

questions.explanation_en: Logarithmic < polynomial < exponential < factorial. Among the polynomial terms, √n = n^0.5 < n log n < n³. And 2ⁿ < n! for large n (for n = 10: 2¹⁰ = 1024 but 10! = 3,628,800).

questions.question_en: For large n, which of the following functions grows the fastest?
questions.explanation_en: Compare base-2 logarithms: log₂(n¹⁰) = 10 log₂ n, log₂(n^(log₂ n)) = (log₂ n)², and log₂(1.5ⁿ) ≈ 0.585n. Since n eventually beats (log₂ n)² (at n = 2²⁰: about 613,000 versus 400), an exponential cⁿ with c > 1 outgrows the quasi-polynomial n^(log n) and every polynomial.

questions.question_en: log₂(n!) is asymptotically equal to:
questions.explanation_en: log(n!) = log 1 + log 2 + … + log n ≤ n log n. Also the top n/2 terms are each at least log(n/2), so log(n!) ≥ (n/2) log(n/2). Hence log(n!) = Θ(n log n); Stirling's formula gives n log₂ n − 1.44n.
i takes the values 1, 3, 9, …, 3ᵏ and the loop stops when 3ᵏ > n. So it runs about log₃ n + 1 times (7 times for n = 1000), which is O(log n), since log bases differ only by a constant factor.
For a given i the inner loop runs i times, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + 20 = 20 × 21 / 2 = 210. In general it is n(n + 1)/2, which is O(n²).
The inner loop runs n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 1 times in total. This geometric series is less than 2n, so the code is O(n). It is not O(n log n), because the log n outer iterations do not each cost n.
The outer loop runs n times. For each i, j doubles from 1 until it reaches n, which takes about log₂ n iterations. Total ≈ n log₂ n, i.e., O(n log n).
The loop continues while i² ≤ n, i.e., while i ≤ √n, so it runs ⌊√n⌋ times. For n = 100 it runs 10 times, so the complexity is O(√n).

i takes the values 2, 2², 2⁴, 2⁸, …, i.e., 2^(2ᵏ) after k steps. The loop stops when 2^(2ᵏ) > n, i.e., when 2ᵏ > log₂ n, so k ≈ log₂ log₂ n. For n = 65536 = 2¹⁶ it runs 5 times (i = 2, 4, 16, 256, 65536).
The two loops run one after the other, not nested, so their costs add: n iterations plus m iterations gives O(n + m). Only nested loops multiply their iteration counts.
i takes the values 1, 2, 4, …, 128 and the inner loop runs i times for each. Total = 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 128 = 2⁸ − 1 = 255. In general this pattern is O(n), not O(n log n).
After k iterations s = 1 + 2 + … + (k + 1) ≈ k²/2. The loop stops when k²/2 > n, i.e., after about √(2n) iterations. Hence the complexity is O(√n).
For a given i the inner loop runs about n/i times. Total ≈ n/1 + n/2 + … + n/n = n(1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n) = n·Hₙ, and the harmonic number Hₙ ≈ ln n. So the code is O(n log n).

questions.question_en: Which type of analysis guarantees that an algorithm will never take more time than a certain bound for ANY input of size n?
questions.explanation_en: The worst-case running time is the maximum time over all inputs of size n, so it is an upper bound that holds for every input. Best case is the minimum (e.g., linear search finding the key at the first position), and average case is the expected time over a distribution of inputs.

questions.question_en: Using the Master theorem, the solution of T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n is:
questions.explanation_en: Here a = 4 and b = 2, so n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂ 4) = n². f(n) = n is polynomially smaller than n² (case 1), so T(n) = Θ(n²).

questions.question_en: Using the Master theorem, the solution of T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n is:
questions.explanation_en: a = 3 and b = 4, so n^(log₄ 3) ≈ n^0.79. f(n) = n log n is polynomially larger (case 3), and the regularity condition holds: 3·(n/4)·log(n/4) ≤ (3/4)·n log n. So T(n) = Θ(f(n)) = Θ(n log n).

questions.question_en: Which recurrence–solution pair is INCORRECT?

options.en: T(n) = T(n − 1) + cn → Θ(n log n)

questions.explanation_en: T(n) = T(n − 1) + cn unrolls to c(n + (n − 1) + … + 1) = Θ(n²), the worst case of quick sort, not Θ(n log n). The other pairs are correct: binary search Θ(log n), merge sort Θ(n log n) and Tower of Hanoi Θ(2ⁿ).

questions.question_en: What is the minimum number of moves needed to solve the Tower of Hanoi puzzle with 7 discs?
questions.explanation_en: M(n) = 2M(n − 1) + 1 with M(1) = 1 gives M(n) = 2ⁿ − 1. For n = 7: 2⁷ − 1 = 127 moves.

questions.question_en: In the optimal (minimum-move) solution of the Tower of Hanoi with 6 discs, how many times does the smallest disc move?
questions.explanation_en: The total number of moves is 2⁶ − 1 = 63. Disc k (k = 1 is the smallest) moves 2^(n − k) times, so the smallest disc moves 2⁵ = 32 times (every alternate move), while the largest disc moves only once.

Let C(n) be the calls made for f(n): C(0) = C(1) = 1 and C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2). So C(2) = 3, C(3) = 5, C(4) = 9, C(5) = 15 and C(6) = 1 + 15 + 9 = 25. This exponential blow-up is why naive recursive Fibonacci is slow.
Each call prints n, recurses on n − 1, and prints n again after the inner call returns; p(0) prints nothing. So 3 2 1 is printed on the way down and 1 2 3 while the calls unwind, giving 3 2 1 1 2 3.
h(4728) = h(472) + 8 = h(47) + 2 + 8 = h(4) + 7 + 2 + 8 = 4 + 7 + 2 + 8 = 21. The function returns the sum of the decimal digits of n.

questions.question_en: An array int A[10][15] (indices start at 0) is stored in row-major order with base address 2000 and 4 bytes per element. What is the address of A[6][8]?
questions.explanation_en: Row-major: address = Base + w × (i × C + j), where C = 15 columns. Address = 2000 + 4 × (6 × 15 + 8) = 2000 + 4 × 98 = 2392.

questions.question_en: An array A[1..8][1..12] is stored in column-major order. The base address is 1500 and each element takes 2 bytes. What is the address of A[5][7]?
questions.explanation_en: Column-major: address = Base + w × ((j − lc) × R + (i − lr)), where R = 8 rows. Address = 1500 + 2 × ((7 − 1) × 8 + (5 − 1)) = 1500 + 2 × 52 = 1604. (Row-major would give 1608.)

questions.question_en: An array A[−3..4][5..14] of 8-byte elements is stored in row-major order starting at address 1000. What is the address of A[2][9]?
An array A[−2..6][−4..3] of 2-byte elements is stored in column-major order with base address 600. What is the address of A[3][1]?
In a one-dimensional array B[5..50] each element takes 2 bytes, and B[12] is stored at address 2114. What is the address of B[30]?
questions.explanation_en: Consecutive elements are 2 bytes apart, so address(B[30]) = address(B[12]) + 2 × (30 − 12) = 2114 + 36 = 2150. The base address of B[5] is 2114 − 2 × (12 − 5) = 2100.

questions.question_en: How many elements does the array A[−4..6][3..12] contain?
questions.explanation_en: Elements in a dimension = upper bound − lower bound + 1. Rows = 6 − (−4) + 1 = 11 and columns = 12 − 3 + 1 = 10, so the array has 11 × 10 = 110 elements.

questions.question_en: Inserting a new element at index 0 of an array that already holds n elements (keeping their order) takes, in the worst case:
questions.explanation_en: All n existing elements must be shifted one place to the right to free index 0, which costs O(n). Accessing an element by its index, in contrast, is O(1).

questions.question_en: A 12 × 12 lower triangular matrix is stored row by row in a 1-D array, keeping only the elements on and below the main diagonal. How many elements are stored?
questions.explanation_en: Row i holds i elements, so the count is 1 + 2 + … + 12 = 12 × 13 / 2 = 78. The 66 elements above the diagonal (12 × 11 / 2) are zero and are not stored.

questions.question_en: The lower triangular part (on and below the diagonal) of A[1..10][1..10] is stored row-wise in a 1-D array starting at address 500, with 2 bytes per element. What is the address of A[7][4]?
questions.explanation_en: Rows 1 to 6 store 1 + 2 + … + 6 = 21 elements, and A[7][4] is the 4th element of row 7, so its offset is 21 + 3 = 24. Address = 500 + 2 × 24 = 548.

questions.question_en: A 7 × 8 sparse matrix has 11 non-zero elements. In the 3-tuple (row, column, value) representation with one header row holding the dimensions and the number of non-zeros, how many rows does the table have?
questions.explanation_en: One triple is stored for each non-zero element (11 rows) plus the header row ⟨7, 8, 11⟩, giving 12 rows of 3 columns (36 values). That is far fewer than the 56 cells of the full matrix.

questions.question_en: In which type of linked list does the last node's next pointer point back to the first node instead of NULL?
questions.explanation_en: In a circular linked list the last node links back to the first, so the whole list can be traversed starting from any node. In an ordinary singly or doubly linked list the last node's next pointer is NULL.

questions.question_en: A non-circular doubly linked list has 8 nodes. How many NULL pointers does it contain?
questions.explanation_en: Each node has a prev and a next pointer (16 in all). Only the first node's prev and the last node's next are NULL; every other pointer links to a neighbour. So there are exactly 2 NULL pointers, whatever the number of nodes.

questions.question_en: A singly linked list keeps both a head pointer and a tail pointer. Which operation still takes O(n) time?

options.en: Insert a node at the end
Insert a node at the front

questions.explanation_en: To delete the last node, the second-last node's next must be set to NULL, and in a singly linked list that node can be reached only by walking from the head, which is O(n). Inserting at either end and deleting the first node are O(1) with head and tail pointers.

questions.question_en: In a doubly linked list, you are given a pointer to a node X in the middle of the list. What is the time needed to delete X?
questions.explanation_en: X's neighbours are reachable through X->prev and X->next, so we set X->prev->next = X->next and X->next->prev = X->prev, then free X. This is a fixed number of steps, i.e., O(1).

f first recurses all the way to the end of the list and prints each node's data only while the calls return. So the last node is printed first and the output is 20 15 10 5: the list is printed in reverse without being changed.

options.en: Reverses the list and returns the new head
Deletes every node and returns NULL
Returns the last node, links unchanged
Makes the list circular and returns head

questions.explanation_en: Each iteration saves the next node in nxt, points the current node back to prev, and then advances prev and head by one node. When head becomes NULL every link has been reversed, and prev points to the old last node, which is the new head.

questions.question_en: Pointer p points to a node of a singly linked list and q points to a new node. Which statement sequence correctly inserts q immediately after p?
questions.explanation_en: q must first take over p's old successor (q->next = p->next), and only then is p linked to q. If p->next = q is done first, the rest of the list is lost and q->next = p->next would make q point to itself.

In each pass p bypasses its successor (p->next = p->next->next) and then moves to the new successor. From 11, node 22 is bypassed and p moves to 33; 44 is bypassed and p moves to 55; 66 is bypassed and p becomes NULL. The list is now 11 → 33 → 55: every alternate node is unlinked.

questions.question_en: Pointers slow and fast both start at the head of a singly linked list of 9 nodes numbered 1 to 9. In each step slow = slow->next and fast = fast->next->next, and the loop runs while (fast != NULL && fast->next != NULL). At which node does slow stop?
questions.explanation_en: fast moves two nodes per step: 1 → 3 → 5 → 7 → 9. After 4 steps fast->next is NULL, so the loop ends with slow at node 1 + 4 = 5, the middle node. The same tortoise-and-hare idea (Floyd) detects a cycle when the two pointers meet.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is an advantage of a linked list over an array?

options.en: Random access to the i-th element in O(1)
Better cache locality of the elements
Less memory needed for each element

questions.explanation_en: A linked list grows and shrinks dynamically, and a node is inserted or deleted just by changing pointers, with no shifting of elements. Arrays win on O(1) random access, cache locality and memory, since every list node needs extra space for a pointer.

questions.question_en: A pile of trays, where the tray placed last is the first one taken off, works on which principle, and which data structure models it?
questions.explanation_en: Last In, First Out (LIFO) means the most recently added item is removed first, exactly like push and pop at the top of a stack. A queue is FIFO: the earliest inserted item leaves first.

questions.question_en: A stack is implemented with an array stack[MAX], and top is initialised to −1. Which condition is checked before a push to detect overflow?
questions.explanation_en: Valid indices are 0 to MAX − 1, so the stack is full when top == MAX − 1 and another push would overflow. top == −1 is the empty (underflow) condition, checked before a pop.

questions.question_en: Which statement about a linear queue is correct?

options.en: Insertion at the front, deletion at the rear
Insertion and deletion both at the rear
Insertion at the rear, deletion at the front
Insertion and deletion both at the front

questions.explanation_en: A queue is FIFO: new elements join at the rear (enqueue) and elements leave from the front (dequeue), so the element that has waited longest is removed first. If insertion and deletion were at the same end, it would behave like a stack.

After 5 enqueues rear = 4 = MAX − 1, and the 2 dequeues only move front to 2. enqueue checks rear == MAX − 1, so it prints Overflow even though q[0] and q[1] are free. This wasted space in a linear queue is why a circular queue is used.

questions.question_en: In a linear array queue, front is the index of the first element and rear is the index of the last element (front ≤ rear). How many elements are in the queue?
questions.explanation_en: The elements occupy indices front, front + 1, …, rear, which is rear − front + 1 positions. For example, front = 3 and rear = 7 hold 5 elements.

questions.question_en: What is the postfix form of the infix expression A + B * C − D / E?
questions.explanation_en: * and / bind tighter than + and −, and operators of equal precedence are applied left to right. So the expression is ((A + (B * C)) − (D / E)), whose postfix form is A B C * + D E / −.

questions.question_en: What is the postfix form of the infix expression (A + B) * (C − D) / E?
questions.explanation_en: The parenthesised parts become A B + and C D −. * and / have equal precedence and associate left to right, so (A + B) * (C − D) is formed first and then divided by E: A B + C D − * E /.

questions.question_en: What is the postfix form of the infix expression A ^ B ^ C * D, where ^ (power) has the highest precedence and is right-associative?
questions.explanation_en: Right associativity means A ^ B ^ C = A ^ (B ^ C), which gives A B C ^ ^. That result is then multiplied by D: A B C ^ ^ D *. Treating ^ as left-associative would wrongly give A B ^ C ^ D *.

questions.question_en: What is the prefix form of the infix expression (P − Q) * (R + S)?
questions.explanation_en: In prefix form each operator comes before its two operands. (P − Q) becomes − P Q and (R + S) becomes + R S, and the outer * is written first: * − P Q + R S.

questions.question_en: What is the prefix form of the infix expression A + B * C ^ D − E, where ^ (power) has the highest precedence?
questions.explanation_en: Precedence gives ((A + (B * (C ^ D))) − E). Writing each operator before its operands: C ^ D → ^ C D, then B * … → * B ^ C D, then A + … → + A * B ^ C D, and finally − + A * B ^ C D E.

questions.question_en: What is the postfix form of the infix expression A * (B + C) − D / (E + F)?

options.en: A B C + * D E / F + −
A B C + * D E F + / −
A B + C * D E F + / −
A B C + D E F + / * −

questions.explanation_en: The sums inside parentheses come first: B C + and E F +. Then A * (B + C) → A B C + * and D / (E + F) → D E F + /. Finally − joins the two parts: A B C + * D E F + / −.

questions.question_en: The prefix expression * + A B − C D is equivalent to which postfix expression?
questions.explanation_en: In the prefix form, * applies to the two sub-expressions (+ A B) and (− C D). So the infix form is (A + B) * (C − D), whose postfix form is A B + C D − *.

questions.question_en: What is the value of the postfix expression 6 3 2 * + 4 −?
questions.explanation_en: Push 6, 3, 2. * pops 2 and 3 and pushes 6; + pops 6 and 6 and pushes 12; push 4; − computes 12 − 4 = 8.

questions.question_en: What is the value of the postfix expression 8 2 / 3 4 * + 5 −?
questions.explanation_en: 8 2 / gives 4, 3 4 * gives 12, 4 + 12 = 16, and 16 − 5 = 11. For each operator, compute (second popped) op (first popped), e.g., 8 / 2, not 2 / 8.

questions.question_en: What is the value of the prefix expression − * + 4 2 3 / 8 4?
questions.explanation_en: Scan from right to left with a stack: push 4, 8; / gives 8 / 4 = 2. Push 3, 2, 4; + gives 4 + 2 = 6; * gives 6 × 3 = 18; − gives 18 − 2 = 16. In infix this is (4 + 2) * 3 − 8 / 4.

questions.question_en: What is the value of the postfix expression 2 3 ^ 4 2 / − 3 *, where ^ denotes exponentiation?
questions.explanation_en: Scan left to right, applying each operator to the top two operands: 2 3 ^ = 2³ = 8 and 4 2 / = 2. Then 8 − 2 = 6, and finally 6 3 * = 18.

questions.question_en: While evaluating the postfix expression 7 3 5 + * 6 8 2 / − *, what are the stack contents (bottom → top) just after the operand 2 is pushed?
questions.explanation_en: 3 5 + gives 8, and 7 8 * gives 56, leaving only 56 on the stack. Then 6, 8 and 2 are pushed, so the stack is 56, 6, 8, 2. Continuing: 8 / 2 = 4, 6 − 4 = 2 and 56 × 2 = 112.

questions.question_en: Starting with an empty stack, these operations are performed: push(4), push(9), pop(), push(6), push(2), pop(), pop(), push(7). What are the stack contents from bottom to top?
questions.explanation_en: push 4, 9 → [4, 9]; pop removes 9 → [4]; push 6, 2 → [4, 6, 2]. The two pops remove 2 and 6 → [4], and push 7 gives [4, 7], with 7 on top.

questions.question_en: The operations push(1), push(2), push(3), pop(), pop(), push(4), pop(), pop() are performed on an empty stack. In what order are the elements popped?
questions.explanation_en: The stack becomes [1, 2, 3]; two pops give 3 and then 2, leaving [1]. push(4) gives [1, 4], and the next two pops give 4 and then 1. Popped order: 3 2 4 1.

questions.question_en: A circular queue is implemented in an array of size N with indices front and rear, keeping one slot empty to tell 'full' from 'empty'. Which condition means the queue is FULL?
questions.explanation_en: Because one slot is left unused, the queue is empty when front == rear and full when advancing rear by one (wrapping with % N) would reach front, i.e., (rear + 1) % N == front. The test rear == N − 1 is the full test of a linear queue only.

questions.question_en: A circular queue is stored in an array of 12 locations (indices 0–11). front = 9 is the index of the first element and rear = 3 is the index of the last element. How many elements are in the queue?
questions.explanation_en: The elements occupy indices 9, 10, 11, 0, 1, 2, 3, which is 7 positions. Formula: (rear − front + N) % N + 1 = (3 − 9 + 12) % 12 + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7.

After four enqueues front = 0 and rear = 3. The two dequeues move front to 2. enq(50) sets rear = 4, and enq(60) wraps rear to (4 + 1) % 5 = 0 and stores 60 in q[0]. So front = 2 and rear = 0, with 4 elements (30, 40, 50, 60).

questions.question_en: A double-ended queue (deque) in which insertion is allowed at only one end, but deletion is allowed at both ends, is called a/an:
questions.explanation_en: In an input-restricted deque, insertion happens at one end only while deletion is allowed at both ends. An output-restricted deque is the reverse: insertion at both ends, deletion at one end only.

questions.question_en: A priority queue of n elements is implemented as a binary min-heap. What are the time complexities of inserting an element and of deleting the minimum element?
questions.explanation_en: Insertion puts the element at the next leaf and sifts it up a tree of height ⌊log₂ n⌋, so it is O(log n). Delete-min removes the root, moves the last leaf to the root and sifts it down, also O(log n). Only reading the minimum (peek) is O(1).

questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT an application of a stack?

options.en: Undo operation in a text editor

questions.explanation_en: Parenthesis checking, undo and function-call management all need the most recent item first (LIFO), so they use a stack. Round-robin scheduling serves processes in arrival order and cycles through them, which uses a (circular) queue.

questions.question_en: Documents sent to a shared office printer are printed in the order in which they arrive. Which data structure suits this print spooler best?
questions.explanation_en: The first document submitted must be printed first, which is FIFO behaviour, so a queue is used. A stack would print the most recently submitted document first.

questions.question_en: A queue is implemented with two stacks S1 and S2. Enqueue pushes onto S1. Dequeue pops from S2; if S2 is empty, all elements of S1 are first popped and pushed onto S2. With n elements, what are the worst-case cost of one dequeue and the amortised cost per operation (tightest bounds)?

options.en: O(log n) worst case, O(1) amortised

questions.explanation_en: A dequeue that finds S2 empty must move all n elements from S1 to S2, costing O(n). But each element is pushed and popped at most twice in its life (once on S1, once on S2), so any sequence of m operations costs O(m), i.e., O(1) amortised per operation.

questions.question_en: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are pushed onto a stack in this order, and pops may be done at any time (the stack is emptied at the end). How many different output sequences are possible?
questions.explanation_en: The number of permutations a stack can produce from n items in fixed input order is the Catalan number Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1). For n = 5: C(10, 5)/6 = 252/6 = 42, far fewer than 5! = 120.

questions.question_en: The elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are pushed onto a stack in that order, and pops are allowed at any time. Which output sequence is IMPOSSIBLE?
questions.explanation_en: To output 4 first, 1, 2 and 3 must already be on the stack with 3 on top, so the next pop gives 3 (or 5 after pushing 5), never 1. Hence 4 1 2 3 5 is impossible. The others can be produced, e.g., 2 4 3 5 1 = push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, push 4, pop, pop, push 5, pop, pop.

questions.question_en: Two stacks share one array A[0..n−1]: stack 1 grows upward from index 0 (top1 starts at −1) and stack 2 grows downward from index n − 1 (top2 starts at n). When does a push cause overflow?
questions.explanation_en: Neither stack is limited to a fixed half; they can grow until they meet. The array is completely full when the next free slot of stack 1 is top2's slot, i.e., top1 + 1 == top2, and then a push to either stack overflows. This uses space better than two fixed halves.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: In a tree, a node that has no children is called a:
questions.explanation_en: A leaf (also called an external or terminal node) has degree 0, i.e. no children. The root is the only node with no parent, an internal node has at least one child, and siblings are nodes that share a parent.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Height is counted as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path (a single node has height 0). The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h is:
questions.explanation_en: Level i (root at level 0) can hold at most 2ⁱ nodes, and a tree of height h has levels 0 to h. Adding 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ʰ gives 2ʰ⁺¹ − 1. The form 2ʰ − 1 is the same fact when height is counted in levels (single node = height 1).

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: What is the minimum possible height of a binary tree with 100 nodes? (Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.)
questions.explanation_en: A tree of height 5 holds at most 2⁶ − 1 = 63 nodes, which is fewer than 100, while height 6 holds up to 2⁷ − 1 = 127. So the minimum height is 6 = ⌊log₂ 100⌋.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: A binary tree has 18 leaves and 10 nodes with exactly one child. How many nodes does the tree have in total?
questions.explanation_en: In every binary tree n₀ = n₂ + 1, so the number of nodes with two children is n₂ = 18 − 1 = 17. Total nodes = n₀ + n₁ + n₂ = 18 + 10 + 17 = 45.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: A binary tree with 30 nodes is stored as linked nodes, each having a left and a right pointer. How many of these pointers are NULL?
questions.explanation_en: There are 2 × 30 = 60 pointers in all. A tree with 30 nodes has 30 − 1 = 29 edges, and each edge uses one pointer, so 60 − 29 = 31 pointers are NULL (always n + 1).

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: How many structurally different binary trees can be formed with 4 unlabelled nodes?
questions.explanation_en: The count is the Catalan number Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1). For n = 4: C(8, 4)/5 = 70/5 = 14.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: How many different binary search trees can be built from the 5 distinct keys 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50?
questions.explanation_en: Every binary-tree shape with 5 nodes can be filled with the sorted keys in exactly one valid BST way (fill it in inorder). So the count is the Catalan number C₅ = C(10, 5)/6 = 252/6 = 42; 5! = 120 counts insertion orders, not distinct trees.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Trees are written as Root(Left, Right); a dash (–) marks an empty child and a bare label is a leaf. What is the preorder traversal of the tree P(Q(S, T), R(–, U))?

options.en: S, Q, T, P, R, U
S, T, Q, U, R, P
P, Q, S, T, R, U
P, Q, R, S, T, U

questions.explanation_en: Preorder visits Root, then Left subtree, then Right subtree. P first, then Q's subtree in preorder (Q, S, T), then R's subtree (R, U). Result: P, Q, S, T, R, U.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Trees are written as Root(Left, Right); a dash (–) marks an empty child and a bare label is a leaf. What is the inorder traversal of the tree M(N(–, O(P, Q)), R(S, –))?

options.en: M, N, O, P, Q, R, S
N, P, O, Q, M, S, R
P, Q, O, N, S, R, M
N, O, P, Q, M, S, R

questions.explanation_en: Inorder is Left, Root, Right. N has no left child, so N comes first, then its right subtree O(P, Q) in inorder: P, O, Q. Then the root M, then R's subtree: S, R. Result: N, P, O, Q, M, S, R.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Trees are written as Root(Left, Right); a dash (–) marks an empty child and a bare label is a leaf. What is the postorder traversal of the tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60(–, 70), –))?
questions.explanation_en: Postorder is Left, Right, Root. Left subtree of 10 gives 40, 50, 20. In the right subtree, 60 has only a right child 70, so it gives 70, 60, then 30. The root 10 comes last: 40, 50, 20, 70, 60, 30, 10.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Trees are written as Root(Left, Right); a dash (–) marks an empty child and a bare label is a leaf. What is the level-order (breadth-first) traversal of the tree 8(3(1, 6(4, 7)), 10(–, 14(13, –)))?
questions.explanation_en: Level order lists the nodes level by level, left to right, using a queue. Level 0: 8; level 1: 3, 10; level 2: 1, 6, 14; level 3: 4, 7, 13. Result: 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: A binary tree is stored in an array with the root at index 1 and the children of index i at 2i and 2i + 1. The filled cells are 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C, 4 = D, 5 = E, 7 = F and 10 = G; all other cells are empty. What is the postorder traversal?

options.en: G, D, E, B, F, C, A
D, G, E, B, F, C, A
D, E, G, B, F, C, A
D, B, G, E, A, C, F

questions.explanation_en: Index 10 = 2 × 5, so G is the left child of E (index 5); index 7 = 2 × 3 + 1, so F is the right child of C. The tree is A(B(D, E(G, –)), C(–, F)). Postorder (Left, Right, Root): D, G, E, B, F, C, A.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Which traversal of a binary search tree lists its keys in ascending order?
questions.explanation_en: In a BST every key in the left subtree is smaller than the root and every key in the right subtree is larger. Inorder visits Left, Root, Right, so it outputs the keys in sorted (ascending) order.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: A binary tree has preorder R T W X Y U V Z and inorder W T Y X R U Z V. What is its postorder traversal?

options.en: W, X, Y, T, Z, V, U, R
W, Y, X, T, V, Z, U, R
W, Y, X, T, Z, V, U, R
Y, W, X, T, Z, V, U, R

questions.explanation_en: Preorder gives the root R; in the inorder R splits W T Y X (left) from U Z V (right). In the left part T is the root with W on its left and X(Y, –) on its right; in the right part U has no left child and V(Z, –) on its right. Postorder of R(T(W, X(Y, –)), U(–, V(Z, –))) is W, Y, X, T, Z, V, U, R.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: A binary tree has inorder 9, 3, 7, 2, 6, 5, 8 and postorder 9, 3, 6, 2, 8, 5, 7. What is its preorder traversal?
questions.explanation_en: The last postorder element 7 is the root; inorder splits it into 9 3 (left) and 2 6 5 8 (right). Working from the end of postorder: 5 is the right root with 2 6 on its left and 8 on its right; 2 has right child 6; on the left, 3 is the root with left child 9. Preorder of 7(3(9, –), 5(2(–, 6), 8)) is 7, 3, 9, 5, 2, 6, 8.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Which pair of traversals is NOT always enough to rebuild a unique binary tree?
questions.explanation_en: Inorder tells which nodes lie left and right of a root, so it fixes the tree when paired with preorder, postorder or level order. Preorder + postorder cannot: A with only a left child B and A with only a right child B both give preorder A B and postorder B A.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The keys 45, 25, 65, 15, 35, 55, 75, 30, 60 are inserted in this order into an empty binary search tree. What is the preorder traversal of the resulting tree?
questions.explanation_en: 45 is the root; 25, 15, 35 go left and 65, 55, 75 go right; 30 becomes the left child of 35 and 60 the right child of 55. The tree is 45(25(15, 35(30, –)), 65(55(–, 60), 75)), whose preorder is 45, 25, 15, 35, 30, 65, 55, 60, 75. The insertion order is this tree's level order, not its preorder.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The keys 50, 40, 60, 30, 45, 35, 33, 70 are inserted in this order into an empty BST. What is the height of the tree? (Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.)
questions.explanation_en: 30 goes left of 40, 35 goes right of 30, and 33 goes left of 35. The longest path is 50 → 40 → 30 → 35 → 33, which has 4 edges, so the height is 4.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: What is the worst-case time to search for a key in a BST with n nodes, and in an AVL tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation_en: A plain BST can become skewed (for example, when keys arrive in sorted order) and then behaves like a linked list, so search is O(n). An AVL tree keeps its height O(log n), so search is O(log n) even in the worst case.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The keys 60, 30, 80, 20, 45, 70, 90, 65, 75 are inserted in this order into an empty BST. The root 60 is then deleted, and it is replaced by its inorder successor. What is the preorder traversal after the deletion?
questions.explanation_en: The tree is 60(30(20, 45), 80(70(65, 75), 90)). The inorder successor of 60 is the smallest key in its right subtree, 65 (a leaf), so 65 moves to the root and its old place becomes empty. New tree 65(30(20, 45), 80(70(–, 75), 90)) has preorder 65, 30, 20, 45, 80, 70, 75, 90.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: How is a BST node that has exactly one child deleted?

options.en: It is replaced by the smallest key of the tree
Its child is deleted along with it
Its only child is linked directly to its parent
The whole tree is rebuilt from the inorder list

questions.explanation_en: A node with one child is bypassed: its parent's pointer is changed to point to the node's only child, which keeps the BST order. Only a node with two children needs its inorder successor (or predecessor) to replace it.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: In an AVL tree, the balance factor (height of left subtree − height of right subtree) of every node must be:
questions.explanation_en: An AVL tree is a BST in which the heights of the two subtrees of every node differ by at most one. So the balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1; a value of ±2 triggers a rotation.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The keys 50, 40 and 45 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. Which rotation restores balance?
questions.explanation_en: After inserting 45, node 50 has balance factor +2 and the new key lies in the Right subtree of its Left child 40, which is the LR case. A left rotation at 40 followed by a right rotation at 50 gives 45 with children 40 and 50.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Taking the height of a single node as 0, what is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 5?
questions.explanation_en: The sparsest AVL tree obeys N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1 with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2. This gives 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, so N(5) = 20. (12 is N(4); 63 would be the maximum for height 5.)

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The keys 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. What is the preorder traversal of the final tree?
questions.explanation_en: Inserting 35 causes an RR rotation at 15 → 25(15, 35). Inserting 55 causes an RR rotation at 35 → 25(15, 45(35, 55)). Inserting 65 makes the root 25 have balance factor −2, so an RR rotation at 25 gives 45(25(15, 35), 55(–, 65)), whose preorder is 45, 25, 15, 35, 55, 65.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Trees are written as Root(Left, Right); a dash (–) marks an empty child and a bare label is a leaf. In the BST 50(30(20(10, –), 40), 70), what is the balance factor of the root 50 (left height − right height), and is the tree an AVL tree?

options.en: +2; it is not an AVL tree
−2; it is not an AVL tree
+3; it is not an AVL tree

questions.explanation_en: The left subtree 30(20(10, –), 40) has height 2 and the right subtree 70 has height 0 (counting edges). The balance factor is 2 − 0 = +2, which is outside −1..+1, so the tree is not AVL.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: In a B-tree of order 7 (each node has at most 7 children), what are the maximum number of keys in a node and the minimum number of keys in a non-root node?
questions.explanation_en: A node of order m has at most m − 1 = 6 keys. Every non-root node must have at least ⌈m/2⌉ = 4 children, hence at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 = 3 keys.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Which statement is true of a B+ tree but NOT of an ordinary B-tree?

options.en: All leaves lie on the same level
Keys inside each node are kept in sorted order
All records are in the leaves, which are linked for range scans
It is a balanced multiway search tree

questions.explanation_en: In a B+ tree, internal nodes hold only index keys; every key and its record pointer appears in a leaf, and the leaves are chained in a linked list, so range queries are fast. Equal leaf depth, sorted keys in a node and multiway balance are shared by both trees.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: A B-tree of order 5 (at most 5 children per node) has height 2, i.e. three levels: root, middle level and leaves. What is the maximum number of keys it can hold?
questions.explanation_en: With every node full, there are 1 + 5 + 25 = 31 nodes, each holding 5 − 1 = 4 keys, so 31 × 4 = 124 keys. In general the maximum is mʰ⁺¹ − 1 = 5³ − 1 = 124.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The array [5, 12, 9, 20, 15, 3, 17] is converted into a max-heap by the bottom-up (heapify) method, starting from the last internal node. What is the resulting array?
questions.explanation_en: Heapify index 2 (9): swap with 17 → [5, 12, 17, 20, 15, 3, 9]. Index 1 (12): swap with 20 → [5, 20, 17, 12, 15, 3, 9]. Index 0 (5): swap with 20, then with 15 → [20, 15, 17, 12, 5, 3, 9]. Inserting the keys one by one would give a different heap.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: The keys 10, 30, 20, 50, 40, 60 are inserted one at a time into an initially empty max-heap stored in an array. What is the final array?
questions.explanation_en: Each new key goes to the end and is swapped upward while it is larger than its parent. After 50: [50, 30, 20, 10]; after 40 (swaps with 30): [50, 40, 20, 10, 30]; 60 swaps with 20 and then with 50: [60, 40, 50, 10, 30, 20].

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: One delete-max operation is performed on the max-heap [90, 70, 80, 40, 60, 50, 75]. What is the array afterwards?
questions.explanation_en: The root 90 is removed and the last element 75 is moved to the root: [75, 70, 80, 40, 60, 50]. It sifts down by swapping with its larger child 80, and at index 2 its only child 50 is smaller, so it stops: [80, 70, 75, 40, 60, 50].

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: What is the worst-case time complexity of heap sort, and is it stable?
questions.explanation_en: Heap sort builds a heap in O(n) and then performs n − 1 delete-max operations of O(log n) each, so it is O(n log n) in every case. Moving elements across the heap can reorder equal keys, so it is not stable (though it is in-place).

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: An expression tree is built for (a − b) * (c + d / e). What does a preorder traversal of this tree give?
questions.explanation_en: The root is the last operator applied, *, with left subtree − (a, b) and right subtree + (c, / (d, e)). Preorder (Root, Left, Right) gives * − a b + c / d e, the prefix (Polish) form; postorder would give the postfix form.

questions.chapter: DSA — Trees, BST, AVL, B-Trees & Heaps
questions.question_en: Using the bottom-up heapify method, building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements takes:
questions.explanation_en: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is O(n). So bottom-up build-heap is linear, even though n separate insertions would cost O(n log n).

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: An undirected graph has six vertices whose degrees are 4, 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation_en: By the handshake lemma, the sum of the degrees equals twice the number of edges, because each edge adds 1 to the degree of each of its two ends. Here 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16 = 2E, so E = 8.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: How many edges does the complete graph K₉ have?
questions.explanation_en: In Kₙ every pair of distinct vertices is joined by one edge, so it has n(n − 1)/2 edges. For n = 9: 9 × 8 / 2 = 36.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: In the cycle graph Cₙ (n ≥ 3), how many edges are there, and what is the degree of each vertex?

options.en: n edges; every vertex has degree 2
n − 1 edges; every vertex has degree 2
n edges; two vertices have degree 1

questions.explanation_en: Cₙ is a single closed ring v₁–v₂–…–vₙ–v₁, so it has n edges and every vertex touches exactly two of them. Check with the handshake lemma: n × 2 = 2 × n edges. (A path graph, by contrast, has n − 1 edges and two end vertices of degree 1.)

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A path graph has 9 vertices. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
questions.explanation_en: A path on 9 vertices has 9 − 1 = 8 edges, so the degree sum is 2 × 8 = 16. Directly: the two end vertices have degree 1 and the other 7 have degree 2, giving 2 + 14 = 16.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A forest (an acyclic undirected graph) has 20 vertices and consists of 4 separate trees. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation_en: A tree with nᵢ vertices has nᵢ − 1 edges. Adding over the 4 trees gives 20 − 4 = 16 edges; in general, a forest with n vertices and k trees has n − k edges.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: For a graph with V vertices and E edges, how much space do an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list need, respectively?
questions.explanation_en: An adjacency matrix always has V × V cells, whatever the number of edges. An adjacency list stores one list head per vertex plus one entry per edge end, i.e. O(V + E), which is much smaller for sparse graphs.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: Which operation is faster with an adjacency matrix than with an adjacency list?

options.en: Listing all neighbours of a vertex in a sparse graph
Checking whether a given edge (u, v) exists
Storing a large sparse graph in little memory
Running BFS over a large sparse graph

questions.explanation_en: In a matrix the cell A[u][v] answers the edge query in O(1), while a list may need to scan all neighbours of u, O(deg u). The other three tasks favour the list, because the matrix always costs O(V) per row and O(V²) overall.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: Breadth-first search and depth-first search are usually implemented with which data structures, respectively?
questions.explanation_en: BFS explores the graph level by level, so it uses a FIFO queue. DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking, so it uses a stack (often the recursion stack).

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: An undirected graph has the edges 1–2, 1–4, 2–3, 2–5, 4–5, 4–6, 3–7, 5–7, 6–7. Neighbours are always taken in increasing order. What is the BFS order starting from vertex 1?
questions.explanation_en: Start with queue [1]. Visit 1 and enqueue 2, 4; visit 2 and enqueue 3, 5; visit 4 and enqueue 6 (5 is already queued); then 3 enqueues 7, and 5, 6, 7 add nothing new. Order: 1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6, 7.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: An undirected graph has the edges 1–2, 1–4, 2–3, 2–5, 4–5, 4–6, 3–7, 5–7, 6–7. Neighbours are always taken in increasing order. What is the (recursive) DFS order starting from vertex 4?
questions.explanation_en: From 4 go to its smallest neighbour 1, then 2, then 3 (2's smallest unvisited neighbour), then 7, then 5 (7's smallest unvisited neighbour). 5 has nothing new, so backtrack to 7 and visit 6. Order: 4, 1, 2, 3, 7, 5, 6.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: What is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges when the graph is stored as an adjacency matrix?
questions.explanation_en: For each of the V vertices taken from the queue, BFS scans its whole matrix row of V cells to find neighbours, giving O(V²). With an adjacency list the same BFS is O(V + E).

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A directed graph has the edges A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→E, C→F and F→E. Which of the following is a valid topological order?

options.en: A, B, D, C, F, E
A, C, B, E, D, F
A, C, F, B, D, E
B, A, C, D, F, E

questions.explanation_en: In a topological order every edge u→v must have u before v. A, C, F, B, D, E satisfies all seven edges. A, B, D, C, … puts D before C (breaks C→D); A, C, B, E, D, … puts E before D; B, A, … puts B before A.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A topological ordering of the vertices of a graph exists if and only if the graph is:

options.en: A directed graph with a cycle

questions.explanation_en: If there is a directed cycle u → … → u, then u would have to come before itself, which is impossible. Every DAG has at least one topological order, found by DFS finishing times or by Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly removing in-degree-0 vertices).

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: An undirected weighted graph on vertices A to F has the edges A–B 4, A–C 3, B–C 1, B–D 2, C–D 4, C–E 5, D–E 7, D–F 6, E–F 3. What is the total weight of its minimum spanning tree?
questions.explanation_en: Kruskal takes edges in increasing weight: B–C 1, B–D 2, A–C 3, E–F 3 (all accepted); A–B 4 and C–D 4 would form cycles, so they are skipped; C–E 5 joins the two components. The tree has 6 − 1 = 5 edges with weight 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 14.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: An undirected weighted graph has the edges P–Q 6, P–R 2, Q–R 3, Q–S 5, R–S 7, R–T 8, S–T 1, Q–T 9. Starting from P, in which order does Prim's algorithm add edges to the tree?
questions.explanation_en: Prim always adds the cheapest edge leaving the current tree: from {P} it is P–R 2, from {P, R} it is R–Q 3, from {P, Q, R} it is Q–S 5 (cheaper than R–S 7 and R–T 8), and finally S–T 1. Total weight 11. Starting with S–T is Kruskal's order, not Prim's.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: What is the time complexity of Kruskal's algorithm on a graph with E edges (using union–find)?
questions.explanation_en: Kruskal first sorts all E edges by weight, which costs O(E log E); the union–find checks that follow are almost constant time each. Since E ≤ V², O(E log E) is the same as O(E log V).

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: How many different spanning trees does the complete graph K₆ have?
questions.explanation_en: By Cayley's formula Kₙ has nⁿ⁻² labelled spanning trees. For n = 6: 6⁴ = 1296. (6⁵ = 7776 and 6! = 720 are common slips.)

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A directed weighted graph has the edges S→A 7, S→B 2, B→A 3, A→C 1, B→C 8, C→D 2, B→D 9, A→D 5. Using Dijkstra's algorithm from S, what is the shortest distance from S to D?
questions.explanation_en: Dijkstra finalises S = 0, then B = 2, then A = min(7, 2 + 3) = 5, then C = min(5 + 1, 2 + 8) = 6, and finally D = min(6 + 2, 5 + 5, 2 + 9) = 8. The path is S → B → A → C → D.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: Dijkstra's single-source shortest-path algorithm may give wrong answers when the graph:

options.en: Is dense, with E close to V²

questions.explanation_en: Dijkstra greedily fixes the distance of the nearest unfinished vertex and never revisits it; a later negative edge could make that distance smaller, so the answer can be wrong. Directed graphs, positive cycles and dense graphs are all handled correctly.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: For a graph with V vertices and E edges, how many times does Bellman–Ford relax every edge, and what is its time complexity?
questions.explanation_en: A shortest simple path has at most V − 1 edges, so V − 1 rounds of relaxing all E edges are enough, giving O(V · E). One extra round that still improves a distance shows a negative-weight cycle.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: The Floyd–Warshall algorithm finds shortest paths between all pairs of vertices. What design technique does it use, and what is its time complexity?

options.en: Divide and conquer; O(V² log V)

questions.explanation_en: Floyd–Warshall builds the answer table d[i][j] by allowing intermediate vertices 1, 2, …, k one at a time (dynamic programming). Three nested loops over V vertices give O(V³) time and O(V²) space.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A connected undirected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if:

options.en: Exactly two vertices have odd degree

questions.explanation_en: An Euler circuit uses every edge exactly once and returns to the start, so each visit enters and leaves a vertex, using its edges in pairs. Exactly two odd vertices give an Euler path (not a circuit) that starts and ends at those two vertices.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A connected undirected graph has the edges A–B, A–C, B–C, B–D, C–D, D–E and C–E. Which statement is true?

options.en: It has an Euler circuit starting and ending at C
It has an Euler path from B to D but no Euler circuit
It has an Euler path from A to E but no Euler circuit
It has neither an Euler path nor an Euler circuit

questions.explanation_en: Degrees are A 2, B 3, C 4, D 3, E 2, so exactly two vertices (B and D) are odd. Hence there is an Euler path that must start at one odd vertex and end at the other, e.g. B–A–C–B–D–C–E–D, but no Euler circuit.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: How many distinct Hamiltonian cycles does the complete graph K₅ have? (A cycle and its reverse count as the same cycle.)
questions.explanation_en: Fix the starting vertex; the other 4 vertices can be arranged in 4! = 24 orders. Each cycle is counted twice (once in each direction), so Kₙ has (n − 1)!/2 = 24/2 = 12 Hamiltonian cycles.

questions.chapter: DSA — Graphs: Representation, Traversal, MST & Shortest Paths
questions.question_en: A directed graph is given by adjacency lists, and neighbours are taken in the listed order: A: C, B; B: D; C: B, E; D: F; E: D, F; F: (none). What is the recursive DFS order starting from A?

options.en: A, C, B, E, D, F
A, B, D, F, C, E
A, C, E, D, F, B
A, C, B, D, F, E

questions.explanation_en: From A go to C (listed first), then to C's first neighbour B, then D, then F. F has no out-edges, so backtrack to D, B and then C, whose next neighbour E is still unvisited. Order: A, C, B, D, F, E.

questions.question_en: In linear search on n distinct elements, if the key is present and equally likely to be at any position, the average number of comparisons is:
questions.explanation_en: Finding the key at position i takes i comparisons, so the average is (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n + 1)/2. For example, with n = 50 the average is 25.5, while an unsuccessful search needs all n comparisons.

questions.question_en: What is the maximum number of key comparisons binary search needs on a sorted array of 1000 elements?
questions.explanation_en: Each comparison halves the remaining range, so the worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons. For n = 1000, ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ = 9 (2⁹ = 512 ≤ 1000 < 1024), giving 10.

questions.question_en: Binary search can be applied efficiently only when the data is:

options.en: Sorted and stored with random (index) access
Stored in an unsorted singly linked list
Unsorted but free of duplicate keys
Spread across a hash table by key

questions.explanation_en: Binary search compares the key with the middle element and discards half the range, which needs the data in sorted order. It also needs O(1) access to the middle element, which an array gives but a linked list does not.

questions.question_en: Binary search for 17 is done on the sorted array [3, 8, 12, 17, 23, 31, 38, 44, 52, 60, 71] (indices 0 to 10, mid = ⌊(low + high)/2⌋). Which elements are compared with the key, in order?
questions.explanation_en: low = 0, high = 10, mid = 5 → 31 > 17, so high = 4. mid = 2 → 12 < 17, so low = 3. mid = 3 → 17, found. The elements compared are 31, 12, 17.

questions.question_en: What are the best-case and worst-case time complexities of binary search on n sorted elements?
questions.explanation_en: In the best case the key is the first middle element examined, so one comparison suffices: O(1). In the worst case the range is halved until it is empty, about log₂ n steps: O(log n).

questions.question_en: Bubble sort with a 'swapped' flag (stop when a pass makes no swap) is given an already-sorted array of n elements. Its running time is:
questions.explanation_en: The first pass makes n − 1 comparisons and no swaps, so the flag stops the algorithm immediately. That single pass is O(n); without the flag bubble sort would still do all O(n²) comparisons.

questions.question_en: What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion sort, and which input causes it?

options.en: O(n log n), for a reverse-sorted input
O(n), for a randomly ordered input

questions.explanation_en: With reverse-sorted input, each new element must move past every element already sorted, giving 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, i.e. O(n²). Already-sorted input is the best case, O(n).

questions.question_en: What is the best-case time complexity of merge sort on n elements?
questions.explanation_en: Merge sort always splits the array into halves (about log n levels) and merges O(n) elements per level, whatever the input order. So its best, average and worst cases are all O(n log n).

questions.question_en: What are the average-case and worst-case time complexities of quick sort?

options.en: O(n log n) and O(n log n)

questions.explanation_en: On average the pivot splits the array into reasonably balanced parts, giving O(n log n). If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, the parts have sizes n − 1 and 0, giving n + (n − 1) + … = O(n²).

questions.question_en: How many key comparisons does insertion sort make on an already-sorted array of 10 elements?
questions.explanation_en: Each of the elements at positions 2 to 10 is compared once with its left neighbour, finds it smaller, and stays put. That is n − 1 = 9 comparisons, which is why insertion sort is O(n) on sorted data.

questions.question_en: Counting sort sorts n integers whose values lie in the range 0 to k. Its time complexity is:
questions.explanation_en: Counting sort makes one pass over the n inputs to count them, one pass over the k + 1 counters to form prefix sums, and one more pass over the inputs to place them. The total is O(n + k), which is linear when k = O(n).

questions.question_en: Radix sort sorts n numbers of d digits each, in base k, using counting sort on each digit. Its time complexity is:
questions.explanation_en: Radix sort performs one stable counting sort per digit, starting from the least significant digit. Each pass costs O(n + k) and there are d passes, so the total is O(d(n + k)).

questions.question_en: What is the maximum number of swaps selection sort performs on an array of n elements?
questions.explanation_en: Each of the n − 1 passes finds the minimum of the unsorted part and does at most one swap to put it in place. So selection sort does at most n − 1 swaps (O(n)), even though it always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons.

questions.question_en: Which sorting algorithm takes O(n log n) time in its best, average and worst cases?
questions.explanation_en: Merge sort's divide-and-merge work does not depend on the input order, so it is O(n log n) in every case. Quick sort degrades to O(n²) in the worst case, and insertion and bubble sort are O(n²) on average.

questions.question_en: How many comparisons does selection sort make on an already-sorted array of 10 elements?
questions.explanation_en: Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted part to find its minimum: 9 + 8 + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 = 45 comparisons. It cannot detect sorted input, so its best case is also O(n²).

questions.question_en: Which of the following sorting algorithms is NOT comparison-based?
questions.explanation_en: Counting sort never compares two keys; it uses the key values as indices into a count array. Merge, heap and quick sort decide the order only by comparing pairs of keys.

questions.question_en: Which of the following sorting algorithms is stable in its standard form?
questions.explanation_en: A stable sort keeps equal keys in their original relative order. Merge sort is stable because, when two keys are equal, the merge takes the one from the left half first. Quick, heap and selection sort can move equal keys past each other through long-distance swaps.

questions.question_en: Which of the following sorting algorithms is NOT in-place in its usual array implementation?
questions.explanation_en: Merging two sorted halves of an array needs an auxiliary array of size O(n). Heap, insertion and selection sort rearrange the elements inside the original array using only O(1) extra space.

questions.question_en: Which group contains only sorting algorithms that are unstable in their standard form?

options.en: Merge sort, insertion sort, bubble sort
Quick sort, merge sort, counting sort
Quick sort, heap sort, selection sort
Heap sort, insertion sort, radix sort

questions.explanation_en: Quick, heap and selection sort all swap elements over long distances, so equal keys can change their relative order. Merge, insertion, bubble, counting and radix sort are stable, which is why each other option contains at least one stable sort.

questions.question_en: Bubble sort (ascending, adjacent elements compared left to right) is applied to [29, 10, 14, 37, 13, 5]. What is the array after the first pass?
questions.explanation_en: Pass 1: 29 > 10 swap, 29 > 14 swap, 29 < 37 no swap, 37 > 13 swap, 37 > 5 swap. The largest element 37 bubbles to the end: [10, 14, 29, 13, 5, 37].

questions.question_en: Bubble sort (ascending, adjacent elements compared left to right, so the largest value moves to the end in each pass) is applied to [8, 22, 7, 9, 31, 5, 13]. What is the array after the second pass?
questions.explanation_en: Pass 1 swaps 22/7, 22/9, 31/5 and 31/13, giving [8, 7, 9, 22, 5, 13, 31]. Pass 2 swaps 8/7, 22/5 and 22/13, giving [7, 8, 9, 5, 13, 22, 31]; the two largest values are now fixed at the end.

questions.question_en: Selection sort (ascending; each pass swaps the minimum of the unsorted part into place) is applied to [42, 17, 63, 8, 29, 51, 3]. What is the array after two passes?
questions.explanation_en: Pass 1: the minimum 3 is swapped with 42 → [3, 17, 63, 8, 29, 51, 42]. Pass 2: the minimum of the rest, 8, is swapped with 17 → [3, 8, 63, 17, 29, 51, 42].

questions.question_en: Insertion sort (ascending) is applied to [27, 9, 34, 15, 6, 40]. Pass i inserts the element at index i into the sorted part on its left. What is the array after 3 passes?
questions.explanation_en: Pass 1 inserts 9 → [9, 27, 34, 15, 6, 40]; pass 2 inserts 34, which stays; pass 3 inserts 15 between 9 and 27 → [9, 15, 27, 34, 6, 40]. After k passes the first k + 1 elements are sorted among themselves.

questions.question_en: How many swaps does bubble sort make to sort [4, 3, 6, 1, 5, 2] in ascending order?
questions.explanation_en: Each adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion (a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]), so the swaps equal the inversions. Inversions: 4 → (3, 1, 2) = 3, 3 → (1, 2) = 2, 6 → (1, 5, 2) = 3, 5 → (2) = 1, total 9.

questions.question_en: Bubble sort (ascending, adjacent elements compared left to right) with an early-exit flag (it stops after the first pass that makes no swap; that pass is counted) is applied to [5, 1, 2, 3, 4]. How many passes are made?
questions.explanation_en: Pass 1 carries 5 all the way to the end, giving [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Pass 2 makes no swap, so the flag stops the sort: 2 passes in total instead of n − 1 = 4. (The direction matters: a right-to-left version that moves the smallest value to the front would need at least 4 passes here, because 5 would then move only one place to the right per pass.)

questions.question_en: Quick sort uses the Lomuto partition on [7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8, 5] with the last element 5 as pivot: i starts just before the array, each element ≤ pivot is swapped into position i + 1 (after incrementing i), and finally the pivot is swapped into position i + 1. What is the array after this first partition?
questions.explanation_en: 2, 4 and 1 are ≤ 5: 2 swaps with 7 → [2, 7, 9, 4, 1, 8, 5]; 4 swaps with 7 → [2, 4, 9, 7, 1, 8, 5]; 1 swaps with 9 → [2, 4, 1, 7, 9, 8, 5]. Finally the pivot swaps with 7 at index 3 → [2, 4, 1, 5, 9, 8, 7].

questions.question_en: In quick sort, the first element 36 of [36, 15, 52, 8, 44, 27, 61, 19] is chosen as the pivot, and the partition step puts the pivot into its final sorted place (as in the Lomuto / Horowitz–Sahni partition). At which position does 36 end up?
questions.explanation_en: After partitioning, the pivot sits at its final sorted position, right after all smaller elements. Four elements (15, 8, 27, 19) are smaller than 36, so it lands at index 4, the 5th position.

questions.question_en: Quick sort always picks the first element as the pivot. Which input makes it run in O(n²) time?

options.en: An array that is already sorted
An array whose first element is always the median
An array with all keys distinct and shuffled

questions.explanation_en: On sorted input the first element is the smallest, so every partition leaves 0 elements on one side and n − 1 on the other. This gives n − 1 levels of recursion and about n²/2 comparisons. Random order or median pivots give balanced splits.

questions.question_en: Two sorted lists with m and n elements are merged into one sorted list. What is the maximum number of comparisons needed?
questions.explanation_en: Each comparison outputs one element, and once one list is empty the rest of the other list is copied without comparing. In the worst case the lists run out together, so m + n − 1 comparisons are made (e.g. 14 for lists of 6 and 9); the best case is min(m, n).

questions.question_en: How much auxiliary (extra) space does the standard array-based merge sort need for n elements?
questions.explanation_en: The merge step copies elements into a temporary array as large as the part being merged, which is O(n) at the top level. This extra space is the main disadvantage of merge sort compared with heap sort.

questions.question_en: What is the lower bound on the worst-case number of comparisons for any comparison-based sorting algorithm on n elements?
questions.explanation_en: A comparison sort is a binary decision tree that must have at least n! leaves, one per possible ordering. Its height is at least log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n), so no comparison sort can beat Ω(n log n) in the worst case; merge and heap sort reach this bound.

questions.question_en: Which sorting algorithm is the best choice for an array that is already almost sorted (only a few elements out of place)?
questions.explanation_en: Insertion sort does work proportional to n plus the number of inversions, so on nearly sorted data it runs in close to O(n). Selection sort stays O(n²), heap sort ignores existing order, and quick sort with a first- or last-element pivot is near its O(n²) worst case on such data.

questions.question_en: Using the division method h(k) = k mod 13, at which slot is the key 158 placed?
questions.explanation_en: 158 = 13 × 12 + 2, so 158 mod 13 = 2 and the key goes to slot 2. (12 is the quotient, not the remainder.)

questions.question_en: The keys 43, 23, 34, 72, 13, 55, 64 are inserted in this order into a hash table of size 10 using h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. Which is the final table (slot:key)?
The keys 22, 33, 15, 26, 4, 37 are inserted in this order into a hash table of size 11 using h(k) = k mod 11 and linear probing. In which slot is 37 stored?
questions.explanation_en: 22 → 0; 33 → 0 taken → 1; 15 → 4; 26 → 4 taken → 5; 4 → 4, 5 taken → 6. 37 mod 11 = 4, and slots 4, 5, 6 are taken, so 37 goes to slot 7. The run of filled slots 4–7 is primary clustering.

questions.question_en: The keys 27, 47, 37, 57, 17 are inserted in this order into a table of size 10 with quadratic probing: probe i uses slot (k mod 10 + i²) mod 10 for i = 0, 1, 2, …. In which slot is 17 stored?
The keys 12, 19, 26, 8, 30, 15, 40 are inserted into a hash table of 7 slots using h(k) = k mod 7 and separate chaining. Which slot has the longest chain, and how many keys does it hold?
questions.explanation_en: 12, 19, 26 and 40 all give remainder 5; 8 and 15 give 1; 30 gives 2. So slot 5 holds the chain 12 → 19 → 26 → 40 with 4 keys, slot 1 holds 2 keys and slot 2 holds 1.

questions.question_en: A table of size 11 uses double hashing: h₁(k) = k mod 11, h₂(k) = 5 − (k mod 5), and probe i uses slot (h₁(k) + i · h₂(k)) mod 11. The keys 14, 25 and 36 are inserted in this order. In which slot is 36 stored?
questions.explanation_en: 14 → 3. 25 → h₁ = 3 (taken), h₂ = 5 − 0 = 5, so slot 8. 36 → h₁ = 3 (taken), h₂ = 5 − 1 = 4, so slot (3 + 4) mod 11 = 7, which is free.

questions.question_en: The load factor α of a hash table that stores n keys in m slots is defined as:
questions.explanation_en: The load factor is the average number of keys per slot, α = n/m; for example, 45 keys in 60 slots give α = 0.75. With open addressing α must stay at most 1; with chaining it may exceed 1.

questions.question_en: In open addressing, linear probing mainly suffers from ______ clustering, while quadratic probing suffers from ______ clustering.
questions.explanation_en: With linear probing, occupied slots form long runs that any new key hashing into the run must walk through (primary clustering). Quadratic probing breaks up these runs, but keys with the same home slot still follow the same probe sequence (secondary clustering); double hashing reduces both.

questions.question_en: Which of the following algorithms does NOT use the divide and conquer technique?
